newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya to host regional summit on Sudan's civil war.
newsitem.headline: Kenya to host regional summit on Sudan's civil war.

text.p: Kenya will host a regional summit next week on civil war in southern Sudan, a government official said on Wednesday.
The official said the meeting of a heads of state committee on Sudan of the regional Inter-Governmental Authority on Development (IGAD) would be held in Nairobi on July 8 and 9.
African diplomats confirmed the summit, to be hosted by IGAD chairman President Daniel arap Moi, and said it would also cover Sudan's stormy relations with neighbouring Eritrea, Ethiopia and Uganda.
"The summit is certainly on and apart from evaluating events in war-torn south Sudan, the leaders will also examine the stormy relations between Sudan and her neighbours," a diplomat told Reuters.
The Kenyan official said Kenya was not particularly keen to keep the IGAD chairmanship, mainly because it was footing the bills for its meetings in Kenya.

The official said the IGAD formula for negotiations between the warring parties in Sudan was for Moi, who chairs an IGAD committee on Sudan, and the presidents of Ethiopia, Eritrea and Uganda to hear in turn from Sudan's President Lieutenant-General Omar Hassan al-Bashir and southern rebel leader John Garang.
The last IGAD meetings involving both Garang and Bashir were held in September 1994.
Direct talks between Bashir and Garang, who heads the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), and an alliance of rebel groups have so far failed to materialise but are seen as a key to peace in Sudan.

Garang's SPLA has fought since 1983 for greater autonomy of the Christian and animist south from the Moslem, Arabised north and has launched a series of successful offensives this year and recaptured a string of towns and villages.
The IGAD summit is also expected to tackle a row between Uganda and Sudan over prisoners of war (POWs).
At talks hosted by Kenya in May, the presidents of Sudan and Uganda agreed to release all those captured in border clashes.
Sudan and Uganda have deep differences over accusations that they each help rebels on their common border.

Last week, Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni told a news conference he would not release more than 100 Sudanese POWs because Bashir had reneged on a promise to help Ugandan rebels release school children they had captured in northern Uganda.
Uganda accuses Sudan's government of arming and giving bases in south Sudan to Ugandan rebels of the Lord's Resistance Army.

Uganda accuses Khartoum of backing Moslem-based rebels of the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) who attacked the western town of Bundibugyo last month. The Ugandan army is battling the rebels in and around Bundibugyo.
The fighting there has displaced more than 30,000 people including up to 10,000 who have since arrived in the towns of Beni and Bunia in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Sudan accuses Uganda of arming and supporting the SPLA.
